title: Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity -- Ch. 16: Death Penalty Cases: A Moratorium on Death
keywords: Catholic Bishops Conference of the Philippines
Article 335 of the Revised Penal Code
primary_topics: Chapter 16 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's survey of the death penalty cases decided from October 11, 1999 to October 10, 2000, written around the eleven-month moratorium on executions for the Jubilee Year that the news dailies reported on March 25, 2000 President Estrada had declared the day before.

The statistical and doctrinal pattern he draws out: only about one third of the death cases reviewed by the Supreme Court were affirmed, over half were commuted to reclusion perpetua, and most involved rape, especially incestuous rape.

The commonest ground of commutation -- the prosecution's failure to allege in the Information or prove beyond reasonable doubt the qualifying circumstances of relationship and of the victim's minority, the subject of the long line of cases from Delos Santos and Mendez through Ferolino, Gianan, Cula, Tipay, Brigildo and Tabanggay.

CJP's abolitionist conviction, argued from the risk of error: Delos Santos shows that even the Supreme Court can make mistakes, and 'Errors in its imposition become nightmarishly irreversible once the appellant is executed' -- 'human reversals do not affect the graveyard,' as they did not for Leo Echegaray.

The other reasons death sentences fell in that year -- unproven aggravating circumstances, conviction for a lesser offense in Campuhan, minority of the offender, incomplete fulfillment of duty, crimes predating the Death Penalty Law, the RA 8294 firearms rulings, and remands for improvident pleas and denied mental examination.

His two procedural interventions of principle: the Genosa remand to receive expert evidence on the 'battered woman syndrome,' and his continuing Dissent, reiterated in Contreras, against reviewing and deciding a death appeal while the appellant remains at large.
sub_topics: The news dailies reported on March 25, 2000 that President Joseph Ejercito Estrada had the previous day declared an eleven-month moratorium on executions, out of respect for the Jubilee Year opened by Pope John Paul II, on the Presidential Conscience Commission's recommendation following an appeal by the CBCP, invoking his power of clemency to reprieve 18 convicts scheduled to die that year.

Under the Death Penalty Law a convict must be executed not earlier than 12 and not later than 18 months after the Supreme Court affirms the sentence; CJP hopes the suspension gives legislators and the people time to consider repealing or amending RA 7659.

He contrasts the muted protest of pro-death advocates against this omnibus moratorium with the 'conflagration' ignited by the Court's January 4, 1999 Resolution postponing Leo Echegaray's execution, when officialdom from the President down demanded the resignation or impeachment of the eight justices who voted for the TRO and justices, employees and their families were threatened, insulted and booed.

The Court nonetheless continued reviewing death sentences, and the 1999 trend held: about one third affirmed, over half commuted to reclusion perpetua, the rest reduced, remanded or acquitted, most of them rape cases.

He sets out the difference between simple rape under the first three circumstances of Article 335 of the Revised Penal Code, punishable by reclusion perpetua, and qualified rape attended by the ten special circumstances added by RA 7659 (effective December 31, 1993) and RA 8353 (October 22, 1997), which he quotes in full.

Failure to allege relationship, case a: in People v. Delos Santos the Court unanimously reopened a final and executory death judgment because the Information nowhere alleged that the accused was the victim's stepfather, and commuted the sentence, doctrines favorable to the accused being given retroactive effect.

CJP calls it fortunate that the defect in the Court's own original Decision was caught before the lethal injection, since the error would otherwise have been literally fatal and irreversible, and recalls having argued in 'Leadership by Example' that Echegaray's death sentence was itself legally erroneous for the same pleading defect.

Case b: People v. Mendez and a line of cases -- Villanueva, Melendrez, Villaroza, Garcia, Magtrayo, Dela Cuesta -- reduced the penalty because 'stepdaughter' and 'stepfather' presuppose a legitimate marriage, while the proof showed only a common-law relationship with the victim's mother.

Case c and d: People v. Cajara found the alleged third-degree relationship unproven, and more than thirty cases from Panique to Nogar reduced penalties where the Informations failed to specify the filial relationship or the victim's age.

In Ferolino, Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. held that alleging the victim was the accused's niece was not specific enough -- the Information had to allege the relationship was within the third civil degree, since even a cousin's daughter is called a pamangkin; Gianan, following Teves, likewise faulted an Information whose syntax could not notify a person of ordinary intelligence of the charge.

Failure to prove age: Brigildo, Tipay, Cula, Licanda, Tabanggay and Canonigo commuted sentences where age, though alleged, was not adequately proven, and Baniguid held that calling the complainant a 'minor daughter' was insufficient because the exact age must be stated.

People v. Dela Cruz accepted the testimony of the victims' mother, who had personal knowledge of her children's ages and was never contradicted, as proof of minority -- relying on Balgos -- after reviewing Javier, Tipay, Cula and Brigildo as cases where proof had failed.

A Separate Opinion, reproduced at length, contended that where the alleged ages fall between 13 and 18 neither the victims' nor their mothers' bare testimony suffices, because in this era of modernism physical appearance cannot gauge age, and because the proof of age 'spells the difference between life and death'; Bawang later reduced a penalty for want of a birth certificate.

Other unalleged qualifying circumstances: Justice Kapunan reduced the penalty in Paramil because the carnapping Information omitted that the driver was killed in the course of the crime and because abuse of superior strength was unpleaded, and Justice Bellosillo refused death in Diaz for want of an information on the sexual assault.

Where the penalty ranges from reclusion perpetua to death, the lower penalty applies absent a proven aggravating circumstance -- so Pedroso (robbery with homicide) and Zheng Bai Hui (drug sale) drew reclusion perpetua, while Gaspar and Gallego went further, holding that dwelling had to be alleged in the Information because 'Any decision authorizing the State to take life must be as error-free as possible.'

Conviction for a lesser offense: in People v. Campuhan, Justice Bellosillo's ponencia found only attempted rape because the prosecution failed to prove penetration of the labia majora -- which CJP reads as a failure of factual proof rather than a doctrinal change.

Juvenile offenders: after the DSWD reported that Gerry Legarda had behaved properly and could be a useful member of the community, the Court referred the recommendation to the trial court of origin, following Galit, as better placed to confirm the youthful offender's reform; and in Lumandong, Justice De Leon Jr. spared an accused who was only 14 years, 8 months and 15 days old.

In People v. Ulep the police-officer appellant was credited with the incomplete justifying circumstance of fulfillment of a duty, a privileged mitigating circumstance under Article 69 that cannot be offset and lowers the penalty; in De Leon the penalty fell because the rape predated the Death Penalty Law's December 31, 1993 effectivity, with sixteen counts dismissed for overly generalized testimony.

The RA 8294 firearms line: Molina, Ringor and Ladjaalam refused to treat illegal possession as an aggravating circumstance or as a separate offense where another crime was committed, the Court holding that penal laws are construed liberally in favor of the accused and that where the law does not distinguish, neither should the Court.

Improvident pleas: Bello, Tizon, Nadera, Abapo and Durango were remanded because a 'searching inquiry' was not conducted -- Justice Melo detailing what such an inquiry demands, Justice Vitug stressing voluntariness and complete comprehension of the plea's effects, and Justice Mendoza chastising counsel de oficio Atty. Manolo A. Brotonel for a cavalier defense; in Estrada Justice Puno remanded because the trial judge had refused a mental examination.

Battered woman syndrome: in People v. Genosa, a parricide convict represented by Counsel Katrina Legarda asked the Court to re-evaluate the traditional elements of self-defense; CJP's Resolution acknowledged the 'legal and jurisprudential lacuna,' ordered a partial reopening for expert psychological and psychiatric evidence, and held that accused persons facing death must be given fair opportunities to proffer all possible defenses.

Review of a death penalty when the appellant has absconded: over CJP's Dissent, reiterated in People v. Contreras, the Court reviewed and acquitted an escaped appellant of the rape of a six-year-old, while dismissing his three reclusion perpetua appeals on the ground that he had made a mockery of the judicial process -- an absurdity, in CJP's view, since the review rewarded the very escape the Court condemned.

stances.claim: The death penalty has no place in the statute books, because errors in its imposition become nightmarishly irreversible once the appellant is executed and human reversals do not affect the graveyard.
stances.rhetorical_move: abolitionist argument from irreversibility, grounded in the Court's own near-miss in Delos Santos and its actual error in Echegaray

stances.claim: Even the Supreme Court can make mistakes, and a death sentence can be imposed and carried out because of one, as happened to Leo Echegaray.
stances.rhetorical_move: institutional self-indictment, using a reopened final judgment as proof

stances.claim: A qualifying circumstance such as relationship or the victim's minority must be both alleged in the Information and proven beyond reasonable doubt before death may be imposed.
stances.rhetorical_move: pattern-tracing across dozens of commuted cases to show the rule's practical force

stances.claim: Where the victim's alleged age falls between 13 and 18, neither her bare testimony nor her mother's suffices; independent evidence of age is required, because that proof spells the difference between life and death.
stances.rhetorical_move: Separate Opinion arguing from a line of precedents against the ponencia in the same case

stances.claim: An accused facing death must be allowed to offer every possible defense, so the battered woman syndrome deserved serious consideration and the Genosa case had to be partly reopened for expert evidence.
stances.rhetorical_move: due process argument filling an acknowledged legal and jurisprudential lacuna

stances.claim: The Court should not review and decide a death appeal while the appellant remains at large; doing so virtually rewards an escape the Court itself calls a mockery of the judicial process.
stances.rhetorical_move: dissent by demonstrated absurdity, pointing to the Court's own inconsistent treatment of the reclusion perpetua appeals in the same case

notable_anecdotes: CJP opens with the March 25, 2000 news reports of President Estrada's eleven-month moratorium, declared out of respect for the Jubilee Year and sparing 18 convicts then scheduled to die by lethal injection.

He recalls the fury after the Court's January 4, 1999 TRO for Leo Echegaray, when almost the entire officialdom demanded the resignation or impeachment of the eight justices who voted for it, and magistrates, Court employees and their families were threatened, insulted and booed.

He recounts the near-miss in People v. Delos Santos, where a final and executory death judgment was reopened on a motion filed January 5, 2000 and the appellant saved from lethal injection because the Information never alleged he was the victim's stepfather.

He revisits his own earlier writing in 'Leadership by Example,' where he had argued Echegaray's sentence was legally erroneous for the same pleading defect and wrote that Echegaray was 'now in the Great Beyond, and no change in jurisprudence can resurrect him.'

He reproduces the exchange from People v. Bello in which the accused explained his guilty plea -- 'I was afraid because, according to them, I will be hanged and I do not want to be hanged because who will support my wife and my children' -- as proof that the plea was improvident.
He notes the Ferolino point that in the Philippines even the daughter of a cousin is called a pamangkin, so alleging a niece relationship is not specific enough to justify death.

He records the DSWD's Final Report recommending that the youthful offender Gerry Legarda be returned to his father's custody, and the Court's decision to send the recommendation back to the trial court under Galit.

He describes the Genosa appellant's plea, through Counsel Katrina Legarda, that after frequent, severe and cruel beatings she was 'trapped in a cycle of violence and constant terror' when she killed her tormentor.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 16 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' surveyed the death penalty cases decided between October 11, 1999 and October 10, 2000, framed by the eleven-month moratorium on executions that the news dailies reported on March 25, 2000 President Joseph Ejercito Estrada had declared the previous day, made out of respect for the Jubilee Year opened by Pope John Paul II, on the Presidential Conscience Commission's recommendation after an appeal by the CBCP, and sparing 18 convicts then scheduled for lethal injection. Artemio V. Panganiban contrasted the muted criticism of that omnibus reprieve with the conflagration that had followed the Court's January 4, 1999 postponement of Leo Echegaray's execution, when officialdom demanded the resignation or impeachment of the eight justices who voted for the TRO. The Court kept reviewing capital sentences, and the trend held: only about a third were affirmed, over half commuted to reclusion perpetua, most of them rape cases. The commonest ground was the prosecution's failure to allege in the Information or prove the qualifying circumstances of relationship and minority -- Delos Santos, where a final judgment was reopened because the Information never said the accused was the stepfather; Mendez and its line, where stepdaughter was alleged but only a common-law relationship proven; Ferolino, where alleging a niece was too vague because even a cousin's daughter is called a pamangkin; and the age cases from Javier through Tabanggay, with a Separate Opinion insisting that between 13 and 18 the mother's word will not do because the proof of age spells the difference between life and death. Other sentences fell for unalleged aggravating circumstances, unproven penetration in Campuhan, the offender's own minority, incomplete fulfillment of duty, crimes predating RA 7659, and the RA 8294 firearms rulings; still others were remanded for improvident pleas taken without a searching inquiry, or for a denied mental examination. He also recorded his Genosa Resolution reopening a case to receive expert evidence on the battered woman syndrome, and his continuing Dissent, reiterated in Contreras, against deciding a death appeal while the appellant remains at large. Throughout he pressed his conviction that errors in imposing death are nightmarishly irreversible, since human reversals do not affect the graveyard.
